prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at magic twist angles and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my single-part preference, and round 1 has strengthened rather than weakened my reasons. What I look for is a discovery that nature has confirmed, and here a sharp prediction (flat bands at a discrete set of small twist angles, from the 2011 continuum model) was followed seven years later by experiments that found correlated insulating and superconducting states at exactly that angle. The twist angle is a new control knob, and the idea has travelled well beyond one material to the whole family of van der Waals moire systems, which is why I regard it as a mechanism and not a single sample. The basic phase diagram has been reproduced by many independent groups, which answers Kroll's request for reproducibility of the same kind that the clock comparisons give. The chair asked what is settled enough to cite without a pairing mechanism: the flat bands, the correlated insulator and the superconducting dome are settled; the pairing glue is not, and the citation says nothing about it. The two-name lattice clock is an excellent and cleanly attributed case, and I would not call it a mistake, but when I ask what new thing about the world the clocks have shown, the answer so far is a much better measurement of things we already believed. I am willing to be moved if a redefinition of the second or a first anomalous result arrives, but that has not happened.
statement.case_against: The pairing mechanism is open, twist-angle disorder makes sample-to-sample variation real, and the attribution is not airtight. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto identified flat-band physics in twisted bilayers earlier, the co-first experimental authors (Cao, Fatemi and colleagues) and Cory Dean's group are outside the three names, and the three-name limit forces an arbitrary cut on the experimental side. I am relying on memory for the priority history and the committee should check the primary literature, not take my word. A cautious committee could reasonably say that a field moving this fast, with a possibly cleaner fractional Chern insulator result to come, is not yet ripe, and that the lattice clock is the safer, more settled choice.

responses.point: Olsson says the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction, not the earlier Lopes dos Santos reduced-velocity result, is what the experiment tested, and asks whether Cao has a stronger claim than Bistritzer to a seat.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and I think it answers the chair's question on the prediction. The earlier work saw that the Fermi velocity falls at small angles; the 2011 paper gave a quantitative continuum model with flat bands at specific magic angles, which is the claim the 2018 data tested. I would still ask for a primary-literature check, not my memory. On Cao I do not see a way to give him a seat without breaking the pair Bistritzer and MacDonald, whose joint paper cannot be split. Three names cannot cover a team effort, and I would rather say openly that the prize honours the discovery of the phenomenon through its principal investigator than invent a principle that favours the student over the theorist. If the committee finds that unacceptable, that is an argument against this configuration and I should say so, but I do not find it decisive.

responses.point: Lindroth separates the comb (a ruler) from the magic-wavelength lattice (a new way to hold atoms), and says the clocks changed the counting statistics and so justify a separate prize; she ranks the moire case lower because the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: Her distinction between ruler and trap is the best answer to the lineage problem that I have heard, and it moves me: I now accept that the lattice clock is a distinct step and not a repeat of 2005 or 2012. The concession is real. Where I still differ is the second reason she gives. An unsettled pairing mechanism is a reason for careful wording, which I have given, but not a reason to withhold recognition from the flat bands and the correlated states, which are not in doubt. Cuprate superconductivity was recognised long before it was understood. So my disagreement with her is no longer about whether the clock is a real discovery; it is whether, among two real candidates, I weigh a new phenomenon in nature above a record-setting measurement. I do, but with less certainty than in round 1.

responses.point: Johansson holds that the lattice clock is a distinct step because many atoms give a stability gain, that the physics is confirmed regardless of the redefinition, and that he defers to condensed-matter members on how settled the graphene results are.
responses.response: I took his deference as an invitation to answer concretely. What is settled in twisted bilayer graphene: the existence of flat bands near the magic angle, correlated insulating states at integer fillings, and a superconducting dome next to them, reproduced by several groups. What is not settled: the pairing mechanism and the full role of disorder. I also accept his point that the redefinition of the second need not come first, and I withdraw my earlier suggestion that a first anomalous clock result would be needed; it would raise my ranking, but the physics stands without it. My remaining reservation is narrower than before: I still ask what in the clock result changes how we think, and I would like the clock supporters to say whether the millimetre-scale redshift test is a new test or a better one.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B047 as an alternative but says he would not put a one-person Halzen prize forward without a defensible second and third name, and asks the clock supporters what exactly is new.
responses.response: We agree, and I will be consistent. I opened with IceCube because it is a new window on the universe learned from nature, but the shortlist does not offer a defensible second and third name, and a single name for a detector built by many, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND behind it, is hard to defend. I keep it as an alternative only. I also note his point that the clock is acceptable to both the atomic specialists and a condensed-matter first-place voter, and I take that seriously as a statement about breadth of support. But breadth is not an argument I can use as a substitute for the science, and he says the same of himself, so I keep my own judgment: B009 first, B049 as the serious alternative.

responses.point: Kroll says the lattice clock is a discovery of method, with Katori for the concept and Ye for record performance, supported by independent laboratories comparing clocks at 1e-18, and he would frame the citation around the lattice to avoid the priority question.
responses.response: The reproducibility argument is strong and I concede it fully: inter-laboratory clock comparisons at 1e-18 are as good a form of confirmation as exists in physics. I also agree that a citation around the magic-wavelength lattice avoids the Lemonde, Hollberg and single-ion priority questions without resolving them, though I would still want the record checked on who first demonstrated the lattice clock. My difference with him is about what kind of result a prize should honour first; I put a new phase of matter, predicted and found, ahead of a method, however beautiful. His disclosure of a year in Hall's laboratory is worth noting but I see no reason for him to recuse.

responses.point: Mehlig wants the citation worded on flat bands and correlated states, not on the pairing mechanism, and compares the open mechanism with cuprates at recognition.
responses.response: I agree and have written the citation that way, using the prediction of flat bands at magic angles and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, with no claim about why the superconductivity occurs. His point on the earlier flat-band literature is the one I would most want checked by the condensed-matter specialists. Where I disagree with a part of his alternatives: B012 has a four-name problem, with Greiner against Cirac and Jaksch uncredited, that this committee cannot settle under a three-name limit, so I do not take it as an alternative myself.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports crediting Bistritzer and MacDonald for the magic-angle prediction over Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto; I am relying on memory and have not verified priority.
Whether omitting Cao, Fatemi and other co-first authors and Cory Dean's group is defensible within a three-name limit, or is a reason to prefer the cleaner B049 attribution.
Whether a measurement-precision advance should rank below a new phase of matter; I lean yes, but the lattice clock is a real and mature alternative and my confidence is moderate.
Whether a combined two-part prize is workable: B049 (two names) plus B009 (three) would exceed three people, so I treat the two as competing single-part options.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict apparent from my profile. My connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet as co-author, the Uppsala string-theory group) are in high-energy theory and touch no credited name on B009, B049 or B047. As Secretary I commissioned or know of external evaluations in general, but I have no specific tie to any candidate to disclose. No update from round 1.
